title: Glare on a forward leg is taken by the transit resolver as the claim, joining two strangers, uncounted; residual glare rate

findings.title: Glare on a forward's leg: R_LEG takes the far exchange's own seizure as the claim and joins two callers, and the transit counts nothing
findings.mechanism:
The resolver watch sets R_LEG on any M on a held leg (net_unit.v:684-687), and w_res then re-points the incoming at that leg and drops the others (:691-705).

There is a window of ~1-3.5 ms between the forwarder's CONFIRM sample of a leg (:779-785) and the leg's write landing plus one turn. In that window the far exchange can seize the same channel for its own origin call or forward. It hunts from the other end, so this needs the link's last free channel.

The far M is then indistinguishable from a claim. Only the origin counts glare (:803); a transit has no n_glare or EV_GLARE path.
findings.trigger: tb_fx sc3: a flood arrives on E30. B's forward confirms S40 free (hst=CONFIRM, h_n=40). The S neighbour seizes S40 for its own call before B's leg write lands.
findings.consequence:
The E flood's caller and the S neighbour's caller are joined both ways (E30 <-> S40), and the flood's other legs, W10 and N74, are dropped. n_glare stays 0 and no EV_GLARE is sent.

The S origin takes our caller's M as its own claim; it is counted there only if inside its guard. Each origin then connects its caller. Neither dialled the other.
findings.realistic: Yes, at real timers. The per-link condition is the same as the documented residual glare: the last free channel, both ends within a few ms. But a flood seizes a channel on every link of the tree, so the exposure per call is multiplied by the number of links it crosses. Order of magnitude: 1e-4 per call in a loaded network (arithmetic).
findings.evidence:
run_fx_sc3.log (work/audit/fwd/):
- :29 '41.630 ms the S neighbour seizes S40'.
- :32: the forward.
- :39 '42.521 rs_busy 01 -> 00': R_LEG.
- :46 '42.959 port 30 latch -> src 40'.
- :54-59: FAIL x4 (joined, hears, backward A follows the S hook, not counted).
- :60 'n_glare 0 -> 0, EV_GLARE 0 -> 0'.

Unchanged with the resolver fix (runfix_fx_sc3.log).
findings.fix:
A real claim can rise only after the leg has been seen BUSY with M low: the far end first holds it to 00, and needs two digits before it can claim. So allow R_LEG only on a leg so armed; that is one flip-flop per leg and can share rs_lb.

An M on an unarmed leg is glare. Count it (n_glare, and EV_GLARE naming the leg). Then either drop that leg and keep the others, which turns the join into a failed branch, or keep the documented 'residual glare joins' but counted. Cost: at most one package.

findings.title: Glare between a transit's forward and an origin makes the upstream call hostage to a stranger; the owner's own claim then releases the path under both callers
findings.mechanism: The forwarder hunts with the same sweep and the same per-candidate g compare as an origin (net_unit.v:759-766), so g protects it equally, and residual glare remains on the last free channel. At the transit the glared leg's M (the far origin's caller) is taken as a claim (R_LEG, net_unit.v:683-686). With one leg (rs_two) the incoming port already listens to the leg (the way back, net_unit.v:732-736), so the upstream origin also sees M rise on its trunk and 'claims' on the stranger's hook (net_unit.v:795-800). From then on it never times out. The resolver frees itself (net_unit.v:701-706). The upstream path is now held up by the stranger's hook through the transit's way back. (i) If the stranger's side drops (hangs up, own code, reserved digit, or its guard), the transit's in-port and the upstream trunk release themselves T_REL later on the fall of their fE/fM. (ii) Otherwise, when the transit's own monitor later claims the upstream call, the CLAIM write re-points the in-port from the glared leg (E up) to 00 (net_unit.v:656-658). Its fE falls, and T_REL later the port releases itself and clears CLM (port.v:183-186, 193). That generalises: any unit write that re-points a port whose E is up becomes a release T_REL later. The release runs back to the upstream trunk. In both cases both origins are 'claimed' and at the last digit connect their callers to trunks that have already released (net_unit.v:818-821).
findings.trigger: tb_pchain.v sc0 (scale 8): chain A 2 2 - B 2 3 - C 2 4, where the B-C link has one channel. A20 dials 1 2 3 2 1 (B21). C20 keys 1 timed so that C's origin and B's forward take B14-C11 unseen. Calibrated from two single keys (B14 written 41.3 ms after A's key, C11 27.3 ms after C's); glare on the first try with C's key 14.0 ms after A's (B14 and C11 both written at 2128.284 ms). Pass 0: the callers dial on 40 ms after C's key. Pass 1: 80 ms after.
findings.consequence: Pass 0: C20's first break fell inside C's 16 ms guard, so C abandoned. C11, B14, B11 and A11 then released one after another while A20 was still dialling. B's monitor cleared, and A's 'claimed' origin connected A20 to the released A11. Pass 1: B's monitor claimed A20's call correctly at b, and the CLAIM write re-pointed B11 off B14 (E up, C20's hook). B11 released 33 ms later, taking CLM, then A11, B14 and C11 followed. A20, who dialled B21 correctly, never reaches it. C20's call went nowhere. Both finish latched onto idle trunks (A20 -> A11, C20 -> C11, both released): silence, and whatever next seizes those channels is heard (the origin slice's S4 listen-in, work/audit/origin/run_s2_5.log). The hypothesised listen-in of C20 on A20's call did NOT happen, because the orphan leg released with the rest. At a hub the resolver would also drop the real legs on the glare leg's M, losing the call in every other branch. At real timers the stranger's M reaches the upstream origin about 15 ms after its seizure, inside the 128 ms guard, so the upstream origin counts EV_GLARE naming its own trunk, a link that never glared (at scale 8 it arrived just outside the 16 ms guard, so this run shows glare 0 at A).
findings.realistic: Residual glare only (see residual-glare-rate): the last free channel must be taken from both ends within about 1.3 ms. The mechanism uses no scaled timer except the guard that triggered pass 0. At real timers the release delays are 256 ms instead of 32, the stranger's departure is a hang-up, own code or reserved digit, and pass 1's self-release happens regardless.
findings.fix: (a) The origin re-checks its claim: after the claim it watches the claimed trunk's M, and if M falls before N_DONE it abandons with NOGO. It already compares the probe's port with d_trunk (net_unit.v:795-797), so this is one more term, and it also closes the origin slice's S4. (b) A resolver treats M on a leg within about 100 ms of writing it as glare, not a claim. A real claim needs two digits, so it cannot come that soon. It then writes that leg away instead of freeing itself; with (a) in place the far origin abandons cleanly. Cost: a small per-resolver age counter, about half a package each. (c) w_claim should also write the one-leg way back away. The general rule: never re-point a port whose E is up unless a release is intended.

findings.title: Residual glare: window about 1.35 ms per end, and rate against load for 2- and 8-channel groups
findings.mechanism: Glare needs both ends to take the same channel after each end's confirm visit (net_unit.v:779-785) and before the other end's M arrives. The per-end window D runs from the confirm visit to the far port's M: the rest of the 1 ms confirm pass (mean 0.5 ms), plus WAIT 156 us and a 133 us word, plus the E capture (mean 0.5 ms), plus the card's 31 us. That is about 1.35 ms mean and 2.7 ms worst. g makes the two ends start from opposite ends of the group, so it needs the last free channel. Forwards count as seizures at each end too, so a central link sees every network flood from both sides.
findings.trigger: Opposite-end seizures within about +/-1.35 ms while exactly one channel is free.
findings.consequence: Estimated glare rate = 2 x P(one free) x lambda_X x lambda_Y x 2D (holding about 8 s mixed floods/calls). 2-channel link: 0.2 E -> 1 per 2000 h; 0.5 E -> 1 per 170 h; 1.0 E (20 % blocked) -> 1 per 33 h. 8-channel link: 2 E -> 1 per 960 h; 4 E -> 1 per 14 h; 6 E -> 1 per 2 h; 8 E offered -> about 1 an hour. Negligible at design loads, but daily-to-hourly under overload on a busy central link. Each event is two joined callers, or forward-glare-collapse. On the counters it shows as EV_GLARE on an origin's trunk even when the glare was hops away.
findings.realistic: Real timing. The window is wiring timing, identical at both scales. tb_lfull and tb_pchain both glared on their first try with synchronised keys.
findings.evidence: Arithmetic on the RTL's confirm-to-write path. tb_pchain glare at try 0 (run_pchain.log); tb_lfull glare at try 0 (work/base-lfull.log 'glare at try 0, B's key 0 us after A's').
findings.fix: None needed at design load. If it matters under overload, keep one channel per group as glare reserve (seize the last free channel only from the g end), about one gate on the sweep's g compare.
